// why: The reference input of the `check-bundle` negative control. Every case beside it is built ON A COPY OF IT, so a case file holds nothing but its own defect. This input MUST pass: were it defective itself, every case would fire because of it rather than because of its own.
// why data, not a real measurement: Building a dozen esbuild probes for each case would cost minutes per run, and with Angular's real builder — quarters of an hour. The same choice as in `check-zoneless` and `check-parts`. The price is visible: the fixtures do NOT exercise the bundling code, they exercise the whole arrangement of checks. Bundling is exercised on every run against the real repository.
// why a fake library: The entrypoints are called `alpha`, `beta`, `kernel` rather than `button`, `select`, `core` — a copy of the real measurement would drift from the repository at every new component, and the fixtures would then need maintenance although they examine nothing that changed. `kernel` is pulled in by EVERY probe (like the real `./core`), it is MIXED — a directive beside its providers, as `./core` has been since D2 — and only `beta` takes that directive, the way only `./select` takes `pctOverlayPanel`. `beta` alone reaches for the CDK overlay (like the real `./select`). `rig` is the plain entrypoint of the `quotes` kind (like the real `./testing`): no component of its own, every other entrypoint's selector in its text as data, held by the metafile alone.
// why a toolchain: The versions the numbers were produced BY, recorded beside them: a size with no tolerance is a promise about ONE toolchain, and the day a compiler moves, the bytes move in the same diff as the reason (`lesson-179`). Fictional here, like every other number in this file.
// why a named probe: What ONE TAG of a multi-tag entrypoint costs (point 12). `./beta` carries two components here, the way the real `./select` carries `pct-select` and `pct-multi-select`: the numbers say the second tag is shed — 500 B of 1400 — which is what a row of the real snapshot reads when the tag nobody imported neither declares `providers` nor is named by the one imported (lesson-173). The reference states the HEALTHY reading, so each case can break one half of it.
// why modules: What each entrypoint's module exports, read by the gate's own `componentRecords` into the TAGS point 12 holds the rows to. Each value says what the key is — a component, a directive, a function or a value — and the label which object: one label is one class, wherever and under whatever key it stands. `./beta` exports `PctBeta` under a second name, `PctB`, that sorts before its own and is not a second tag, and a directive beside its two components, the way the real `./select` exports `PctSelectOptionTemplate`. The primary re-exports the kernel's provider as the very object the kernel exports, the way `.` re-exports `providePctConfig` from `./core`, and exports a value that is `null`, which the reader passes over without reading a definition off it. The keys are written out of order on purpose: the case builder lists them in code-unit order, as a module namespace does. The row of `./beta` records `PctBeta` as the key its probe imported, the second of the class's keys: a row may import its class under any of them.
